events.text: Through a gap in the clouds you can see the mountain where you trained, centuries ago. There is a path up it now, worn knee-deep into the rock by pilgrims. Every spring they climb it in a long line of straw hats. At the top they bow to an empty hut. Yours.
events.arc: The Pilgrims on the Old Path

choices.text: Let a warm wind meet them at the top

effects.log: The wind comes out of nowhere and smells of pine and rice smoke. The pilgrims take off their hats. A very old pilgrim sits down and cries, happily.

choices.text: Count the hats, as you once counted roof tiles

effects.log: Four hundred and six. Last spring it was three hundred and ninety. The line grows every year. You are not sure what they come for. Perhaps the climb.

choices.text: Close the clouds; the hut is theirs now

effects.log: Whatever they find up there, they bring it with them. You leave them to it. The hut, you notice, has a new roof.

events.text: One pilgrim did not stop at the hut. A thin old woman has kept climbing, past the last tree, past the snow, into the clouds themselves. She is sitting on the last rock of the world below with a bowl of rice, waiting, as if for a friend who is late.
events.arc: The Pilgrim Who Climbed Too High

choices.text: Go down the cloud stair and sit with her

effects.log: She is not surprised. "You took your time," she says, and shares the rice. She talks about her sons. You listen until her bowl is empty and she starts home.

choices.text: Send a crane to guide her safely down

effects.log: The crane walks ahead of her on the ice, step by step, all the way to the tree line. She bows to it at the bottom. It bows back. You taught it that.

choices.text: Watch, and learn what patience looks like

effects.log: She waits all day without fidgeting once. At dusk she nods, as if something was answered, and goes. You have meditated for a thousand years. She is better at it.

events.text: Smoke rises to your isle with words in it. Two righteous sects below have burned one petition together, which they have not done in three centuries. They quarrel over a spring both claim you blessed. They ask you, the oldest name the murim still prays to, to judge.

choices.text: Send both heads the same dream

effects.log: In the dream you are both of them, drinking from the spring, thirsty. They wake on the same morning and meet halfway. The spring is shared now. Mostly.

choices.text: Rule for the poorer sect

effects.log: The rich sect is outraged for a decade and then builds a better well. Both are fine. The poorer sect names its well-bucket after you.

choices.text: Refuse: they must learn to judge

effects.log: No answer comes back up. Down below, two old heads sit on a rock by the spring for nine days and work it out themselves. It holds better than a ruling would have.

events.text: A crane brings a scroll so long it trails behind the bird like a tail. It is the lineage of the one pupil you taught below, copied by every generation since. Teacher to student, teacher to student. Generation after generation. Your name is at the top. Every other name is a stranger.

choices.text: Read every name, slowly

effects.log: It takes all day. Generation nine had a sense of humour: there is a cat in the margin. Generation twenty wrote very small, to save paper. You know them a little now.

choices.text: Add one line at the bottom, in your hand

effects.log: You write: Breathe first. The crane takes it back down. The next generation will have a very confusing morning.

choices.text: Roll it up and keep it by your bed

effects.log: Some nights, when eternity is very large, you unroll a little of it. All those people, all because one pupil kept turning up.

events.text: Below, at a pass you once swore to guard, a bell is rung every year on the day you made the oath. You guarded it for sixty years and then you ascended. The pass is a market town now. They still ring the bell. Nobody there remembers why, only that it is important.

choices.text: Ring a bell up here at the same moment

effects.log: Two bells, one above the clouds and one below. For one breath they ring together. In the town a dog howls, and a child asks what that echo was.

choices.text: Release the town from the old oath

effects.log: You send a dream to the bell-ringer: the pass is safe, the oath is kept. Next year they ring the bell anyway. It is a festival now. Oaths become festivals, if you are lucky.

choices.text: Look at what the town has become

effects.log: Noodle stalls, a horse fair, a terrible inn. Nobody has fought on the pass for centuries. That was the point of guarding it.

events.text: You part the clouds and do not recognise the country. The great river has a canal beside it now, straight as a ruler. Woodblock books are sold in every market. Farmers wear hats in a shape you have never seen. Somewhere in all of it is the village you were born in.
events.arc: The World Has Moved the Furniture

choices.text: Find the village

effects.log: It takes a week of looking. The well is still there. The rest is a dye works, purple to the elbows. You find you do not mind.

choices.text: Study the new world like a manual

effects.log: Canals, presses, banks, a new kind of plough. None of it uses qi. All of it is clever. You were never the only clever thing in the world.

choices.text: Let it be strange

effects.log: You let the clouds close. Centuries are long enough to earn not understanding a hat.

events.text: In meditation you try to name one living person below who has seen your face. Not your statue. Your face. You go through every name you know. Every one is a grave, or a grave's grandchild's grave. The list is empty.

choices.text: Sit with the emptiness until it changes

effects.log: It is cold for a long time. Then it is only quiet. The faces are not gone. They are in how you hold a cup, how you bow. You carry them. That will do.

choices.text: Write the faces down from memory

effects.log: You draw them badly, one a night. A hundred nights. The face of the cook who fed you as a child comes out best. You always did like her.

choices.text: Go and find someone new to know

effects.log: There is a young immortal on the next isle who talks too much. You let it talk. It is a start.

events.text: The great statue of you at Mount Song is recarved every century. You watch the masons this time. The new face is the face of the current emperor, who paid for the stone. The emperor has a weak chin. Your statue now has a weak chin.
events.arc: The Statue Gets a New Face

choices.text: Laugh until the isle shakes

effects.log: An earthquake is recorded below, small, centred on nothing. The chroniclers are puzzled. You are, for the first time this century, delighted.

choices.text: Crack the chin with a small, careful storm

effects.log: One bolt, very precise. The masons are told it was heaven's judgement on the chin. They carve a better one. It still is not yours, but it is a chin.

choices.text: Leave it; the statue is not you

effects.log: People pray to it and feel better. That is what it is for. Your face was never the useful part.

events.text: A drought broke below on the day a farmer prayed to you, and since then every child in that county has been given your name. There are six hundred of you now. Small ones, loud ones, one who has stolen a goose. All of them answer to your name when their mothers shout it.

choices.text: Watch over the goose thief

effects.log: The goose thief grows up to be a magistrate, a fair one. You take no credit. You may have nudged the goose.

choices.text: Send rain to the county again

effects.log: Another good harvest. Another wave of babies with your name. At this rate the whole province will answer when anyone calls you.

choices.text: Listen to them all being called for supper

effects.log: At dusk the whole county shouts your name, house by house. You have never been so wanted. None of them mean you. All of them mean you.

events.text: A band below has taken your name for its banner. They call themselves your true heirs, burn villages that will not pay, and say the old master commands it. This year their leader has done something new: climbed into the clouds on stolen arts, to ask you for your blessing in person.

choices.text: Meet the leader on the cloud stair

ok.log: You do not strike. You only stand there being who you are. The leader's arts fail, one by one, like candles in wind. The banner falls apart within the year.

fail.log: Stolen arts can still bite. You take a wound to the shoulder before the leader flees back down. The band breaks up anyway: its leader told them the old master smiled.

choices.text: Speak to the band in a dream, all at once

effects.log: Two hundred bandits wake from the same dream of an old master shaking a head, very slowly. Half of them go home. The other half are arrested by the East Gate militia, who had the same dream.

choices.text: Send word to the great sects below

effects.log: A crane, a letter, a seal they still recognise. The sects ride within a month. You watch from above. It is strange to be someone's reason.

variants: A band of raiders below has made your name its banner: your true heirs, they say, and they burn the villages that will not pay. Now their leader has climbed into the clouds on stolen arts, to ask for your blessing face to face.

Below, men who burn villages carry your name on their flag and swear you command it. This year the boldest of them has come up the cloud stair, stolen arts and all, to kneel and ask you to bless the work.

events.text: Someone has ascended recently and been told the stories. The legend from the world below, older than most sects. Now that person is at the edge of your isle with a drawn sword and very bright eyes, asking to cross blades with the legend, once, for the honour of it.
events.arc: The New Immortal Wants a Fight

choices.text: Cross blades, once

ok.log: One exchange. You touch the newcomer's sword with yours and the sword stops wanting to be swung. They bow so low their hat falls off.

fail.log: They are better than they look. They nick your sleeve and the arm under it. You laugh, which they find more frightening than losing would have been.

choices.text: Offer tea first and a fight after

effects.log: By the third cup they have stopped holding the sword. By the fifth they are telling you about their mother. The fight is postponed. Indefinitely.

choices.text: Point them at a harder opponent

effects.log: "The immortal on the north isle is older than me and much ruder." They go. You hear the clash from here. You put the kettle on for later.

variants: A newly ascended immortal has heard the stories: the legend from below, older than most sects. Now they stand at the edge of your isle, sword drawn, eyes very bright, asking to cross blades with you once, for the honour.

Someone new to the clouds has been told who you are, and has come straight to your isle with a drawn sword and no sense at all. One exchange, they ask, only one, so they can say they crossed blades with the legend.

events.text: Three young immortals have made a wager about you. Each thinks a different one of the old stories is true: that you never draw your sword, that you cannot be surprised, that you once split a waterfall. They have come to test all three at once, by ambush.

choices.text: Let them try, and keep the sword sheathed

ok.log: Story one: true. Story two: true, they were very loud in the bushes. Story three you demonstrate on a cloud, which splits nicely. Everyone pays everyone.

fail.log: Story two turns out to be false. One of them lands a kick. You are delighted, and sore, and nobody knows how to settle the wager now.

choices.text: Tell them which stories are true

effects.log: Only the waterfall one, and it was a small waterfall. They are disappointed. Then they are not, and you spend the evening telling them the real ones, which are better.

choices.text: Make a wager of your own

effects.log: That they cannot sit still for a day. They cannot. You win three peaches and a great deal of respect.

variants: Three young immortals have a wager about you. One says you never draw your sword, one that you cannot be surprised, one that you once split a waterfall. They mean to test all three stories at once, by ambush.

A wager among three young immortals: is it true you never draw, never startle, and once cut a waterfall in two? They have decided an ambush will settle all three, and they are not as quiet as they think.

events.text: {npc} ascended from the world below in the same century you did. Everyone else from that century has gone on, or faded, or wandered past the Heaven's Gate. There are two of you left who remember the old murim. {He} comes once a generation to drink tea and complain about the young.
events.arc: Tea With the Only Other One

choices.text: Complain about the young together

effects.log: Two thousand years old and still certain that people used to bow better. It is very comforting. {npc} leaves in a fine mood.

choices.text: Ask {him} what {he} still wants

effects.log: {He} thinks for a long time. "To be surprised," {he} says. You try. You fail. {He} is surprised that you tried, which counts.

choices.text: Recite the names of the old masters together

effects.log: Name for name, back and forth, until the stars come out. Two people keeping a whole world alive by saying it aloud.

events.text: The proverbs carved over the sect gates below are mostly yours, or so the carvers say. You read them through the clouds. The one about patience is yours. The one about mercy is yours. The one about never eating fish on a festival day you have never seen before in your life.

choices.text: Find out who really said it

effects.log: A cook, seventeen hundred years ago, who did not like gutting fish on holidays. A sensible person. You decide to let them have your name. It was a good proverb.

choices.text: Send a dream to correct it

effects.log: The head of the Alliance wakes and has the fish proverb removed from one gate. There is a scandal. It is put back. You give up.

choices.text: Write a new one, a true one

effects.log: You drop it through the clouds on a feather: Breathe before you answer. It is carved within a year, attributed to an obscure monk.

events.text: The last practitioner of your sword style is dying below, in a small room above a rice shop. A plain old man who taught it to no one because no one asked. When he goes, the style goes with him. Nobody below knows. You know.

choices.text: Send him a dream of the whole style, perfect

effects.log: In the dream you do the forms together, all of them, slowly. He smiles at the last one. In the morning the rice-seller's boy finds him with his hands in the opening stance.

choices.text: Send a crane to the rice-seller's boy

effects.log: The crane walks into the shop and refuses to leave until the boy goes upstairs. The old man teaches him one form before the end. One form is enough to start a style.

choices.text: Let the style end with grace

effects.log: Styles are born and die like people. Yours had nearly two thousand years. You sit very still while he goes, and then you practise it once, alone, for him.

events.text: A southern province counts its years from the day you ascended. This is the year one thousand and something After the Master. Their almanac has a page about you: your birthday (wrong), your favourite food (wrong) and the day you will return (soon, apparently, every year).

choices.text: Return, briefly, in a dream to the almanac-maker

effects.log: You correct the birthday. The almanac-maker is so overjoyed the new edition says you will return next spring. You let it stand.

choices.text: Send the favourite food as a sign

effects.log: A steamed bun falls from a clear sky into the governor's lap. The governor eats it. The province declares the day a holiday.

choices.text: Smile and let them keep counting

effects.log: A calendar is a promise that someone will remember. They are keeping it. You do not need to be right about the buns.

events.text: Long ago, before you ascended, you defeated a tyrant. The tyrant's youngest child swore to repay it. That child cultivated, survived, ascended, and has spent every century since getting ready. Today {npc} is at the edge of your isle, white-haired, very polite, and ready.

choices.text: Accept the duel the oath demands

ok.log: It is the best fight of the millennium. You win. {npc} sits down in the moss and laughs, the first laugh in a thousand years. "Done," {he} says. "At last."

fail.log: {npc} has had well over a thousand years to study your one weakness. It works. {He} stops a hair from finishing it, and bows. "That is enough. I only wanted to know I could."

choices.text: Tell {him} what the tyrant really did

effects.log: {npc} knew. {He} has always known. {He} sits down anyway and listens to all of it, and at the end {he} unbuckles the sword and leaves it on your step.

choices.text: Ask what {he} will do after

effects.log: {npc} has never thought about after. You both sit there, thinking about it. In the end {he} goes off to learn the zither. You get a terrible letter about it every decade.

events.text: The rules of the murim have changed below, century by century. Things you were taught were wicked are law now. Things you were taught were good are crimes. You have not moved at all. You meditate on which of you is lost.

choices.text: Hold to what you were taught

effects.log: Mercy, honesty, a straight back. Most of it still holds. The rest was about hats. You keep the first part and let the hats go.

choices.text: Learn the new rules with an open mind

effects.log: Some of the new ones are better. They feed orphans now as law, not charity. You were wrong about one or two things, two thousand years ago. It is a relief.

choices.text: Find what never changed under all of it

effects.log: Under the rules there is only this: do not make people smaller. It was true when you were born. It is true now.

events.text: A festival below is held in your honour. You watch the whole thing through the clouds: masked dancers, drums, a dragon made of forty people. They are dancing your life. In this version you killed a dragon. In real life you shared a meal with one.

choices.text: Send lanterns up into the sky for them

effects.log: A thousand lanterns rise that nobody lit. The crowd goes wild. Next year the dance has a new scene: the master lights the sky.

choices.text: Visit the dancers in a dream to tell the true story

effects.log: Next year the dragon and the master sit down together in the last scene and eat noodles. Half the audience hates it. The children love it.

choices.text: Enjoy the version where you win

effects.log: It is a very good dragon. You win very convincingly. After two thousand years you are allowed one flattering festival.

events.text: A tribulation cloud has gathered over the next isle, where a young immortal is breaking through. It is far too big for one so new. The young one has seen it too, and is sitting very straight, very pale, waiting for the first bolt.
events.arc: A Tribulation Meant for Someone Else

choices.text: Stand under the cloud beside them

ok.log: The first six bolts find two heads instead of one and do not know which to choose. The last three you take on your palm. The young one breaks through, shaking, alive.

fail.log: The cloud does not like being shared. It gives you a bolt of your own for the trouble. The young one breaks through. You smell of burnt hair for a month.

choices.text: Shout the old trick across: breathe out on the strike

effects.log: You learned that a very long time ago, on a hill in the rain. The young one breathes out. The bolts pass through like light through water.

choices.text: Ring your bell to split the cloud

effects.log: An old array, an old bell. The cloud splits in two and wanders off, grumbling, to fall on an empty sea.

variants: Over the next isle a tribulation cloud has gathered for a young immortal's breakthrough, far too big for one so new. The young one has seen it, and sits very straight and very pale, waiting for the first bolt.
Next door, a young immortal is breaking through, and the cloud Heaven has sent is the size of a fortress. The young one sits under it, white to the lips, back straight, waiting for the first strike.

events.text: There is a fallen immortal who feeds on fame. Not on flesh: on the prayers that rise to the famous. {npc} drifts from isle to isle, drinking other immortals' worship until they fade. This year {he} has noticed how much incense rises to you.

choices.text: Face {him} openly

ok.log: You stand in your own smoke and let {npc} try to drink it. It is too much: centuries of grandmothers and pilgrims and children. {He} chokes on it and flees, smaller.

fail.log: {npc} takes a long swallow of your prayers before you break {his} grip. For a season the incense below tastes thin. Then it comes back, stubborn as the people sending it.

choices.text: Give the prayers away before {he} can drink them

effects.log: You send every prayer back down as rain on the people who sent it. There is nothing left on your isle to steal. {npc} leaves, puzzled, very hungry.

choices.text: Ask what {he} was before

effects.log: A village god, once, forgotten when the village was. {He} has been hungry ever since. You do not cure it. You sit with {him} a while, which nobody has done in an age.

variants: A fallen immortal who feeds on fame drifts from isle to isle: {npc}, who eats not flesh but the prayers that rise to the famous, until they fade. This year {he} has noticed how much incense rises to you.
There is a hunger loose among the isles: {npc}, a fallen immortal who drinks the worship of others until nothing is left of them, and {he} has been watching the smoke that rises to you.

events.text: Long ago, below, you sealed something under a mountain: a beast of old poison that ate villages. The seal was meant to outlast you. It has outlasted everyone else. This spring it cracked. The beast is digging toward the shrine town that prays to you.

choices.text: Go down the cloud stair and set the seal again

ok.log: You stand on the mountain for the first time in centuries and press the old seal shut with both hands. The shrine town never knows how close it came.

fail.log: The beast has grown in the dark. Sealing it again costs you a wound that will not close for years. The seal holds. It will hold a long time.

choices.text: Wake the town in a dream and send it up the valley

effects.log: Everyone dreams of the same red mountain and leaves before dawn, with the goats. The beast breaks out into an empty town, finds nothing, and goes back to sleep.

choices.text: Teach the shrine monks to mend the seal

effects.log: Seven monks, one dream a night, for a season. They mend it. The town has guardians of its own now. You should have done that the first time.

variants: Long ago, below, you sealed a beast of old poison under a mountain. The seal has outlasted everyone but you, and this spring it cracked. The beast is digging towards the shrine town that prays to you.
The seal you set under a mountain in your first life has cracked at last. Below it the old poison beast is awake and digging, and the nearest town is the one that keeps your shrine.

events.text: On festival nights the sky lanterns from below drift up past your isle, and lately someone has been netting them: cloud raiders on a drifting rock, stealing the wishes inside to sell at the heavenly market. Tonight their nets are out again.

choices.text: Cut the nets and send the raiders running

ok.log: Three slashes, three nets, a sky full of freed lanterns. The raiders pole their rock away very fast. The wishes go on up, wherever wishes go.

fail.log: The raiders have a net for immortals too. You spend an undignified hour in it before you tear free. Most of the lanterns get away while they are busy with you.

choices.text: Light a false lantern to lure them off

effects.log: One huge golden lantern, drifting the wrong way. The raiders chase it over the horizon. It contains a note: Go home.

choices.text: Buy the stolen wishes back and let them go

effects.log: You pay in peaches. The raiders think you are mad. You open the sack on the edge of your isle and a hundred small wishes float up, one about a lost cat.

variants: On festival nights the lanterns of the world below float up past your isle, and lately someone has been netting them: raiders on a drifting rock, who sell the wishes inside at the heavenly market. Their nets are out tonight.
The sky lanterns are rising from below again, a festival night, and again the raiders' drifting rock is waiting in their path with nets spread, to steal the wishes and sell them above.

events.text: Enforcers of the Jade Court arrive with a writ. Immortals are forbidden to meddle below, and the Court has kept count: rain sent, dreams sent, a storm on a warlord. You have answered too many prayers. The writ says you will come with them.
events.arc: A Writ From the Jade Court

choices.text: Refuse, and stand your ground

ok.log: The enforcers try. The enforcers sit down. The writ is withdrawn, quietly, with a note that the Court would be glad of your company at a banquet, at your leisure.

fail.log: There are a great many enforcers. You spend a season in a very comfortable cell on a pearl isle, and come out with a warning and a much better understanding of the Court.

choices.text: Go with them and argue your case

effects.log: You argue for nine days. You quote the Court's own founding law, which nobody has read in an age. The writ is torn up. You are invited back to argue more.

choices.text: Promise fewer miracles, and keep it, mostly

effects.log: Fewer miracles. Smaller ones. A feather instead of a storm. The prayers below are answered more quietly now. You find quiet answers work rather well.

variants: Jade Court enforcers arrive with a writ. Immortals may not meddle below, and the Court has counted: rain sent, dreams sent, one storm on a warlord. Too many answered prayers. You are to come with them.

A writ of the Jade Court, carried by enforcers who do not sit down: rain, dreams, a storm on a warlord, every one of your answers to the world below written up as a breach. They have come to take you in.

events.text: A village school below has a custom: every child, on the first day, writes a letter to you and burns it at the shrine. The smoke brings them up all at once, forty small letters. Most ask for good marks. One asks whether immortals have to do homework.

choices.text: Answer the homework one in a dream

effects.log: Yes, you tell the child, forever, and it never gets easier. The child wakes very pleased to have been answered, and very worried about forever.

choices.text: Read every letter twice

effects.log: Forty children, forty handwritings, one spelling of your name that is very creative. You keep them in a box with last year's.

choices.text: Send the whole class one good harvest of luck

effects.log: Everyone passes. The teacher is suspicious. The teacher, you notice, also burned a letter, asking for patience. You send a little of that too.

events.text: A whole province below has had no rain for three years. Its governor has ordered every temple to pray to you, by decree, at noon each day. The smoke is so thick around your isle that the other immortals have complained about the smell.

choices.text: Send rain, a lot of it

effects.log: Three days of rain. The governor takes the credit. The farmers know better and leave rice cakes at the shrine for a decade.

choices.text: Show a farmer where the deep water lies

effects.log: One dream, one shovel, one very deep well. Then forty wells. The province never fears a drought again. It stops praying to you so much. That is fine.

choices.text: Ask the cloud immortals why it stopped

effects.log: A rain spirit has been sulking over an insult four hundred years old. You apologise on the province's behalf. It rains on the spot.

events.text: Through the clouds you hear children below singing a skipping song. It is the one you sang at six in a dusty lane, word for word, except the last verse, which now has your own name in it, and says you can fly.

choices.text: Hum along the whole way through

effects.log: You still know every word, even the new verse, which you have never heard. Six years old and a thousand, singing the same song in two places.

choices.text: Sit with what has lasted

effects.log: Empires, sects, styles and famous names have come and gone. A skipping song in a dusty lane has outlasted them all. You take note of what lasts.

events.text: Prayers to you are being answered, and you are not the one answering them. {npc}, a minor immortal, has set up on a cloud bank below yours and is catching your prayers as they rise, answering the easy ones in your name, and keeping the offerings.

choices.text: Go down and have it out

ok.log: A short, sharp lesson on a cloud bank. {npc} flees with no offerings and a new respect for the old names.

fail.log: {npc} fights dirty and fast. You win, but with a black eye that the other immortals find very funny for a season.

choices.text: Let {him} keep the easy ones, and check the work

effects.log: {npc} is lazy but not cruel. Lost cats found, rain on time. You let {him} carry on, and take the hard prayers yourself. Somebody has to start small.

choices.text: Hire {him} properly

effects.log: {npc} is so startled to be offered honest work that {he} does it very well. You have an assistant now. The prayers are answered faster than ever.

variants: Someone else is answering your prayers. {npc}, a minor immortal, has settled on a cloud bank below yours, catching the prayers as they rise, answering the easy ones in your name and keeping the offerings.
The prayers to you are being answered, quickly and not very well, by {npc}: a minor immortal on a cloud bank just under your isle, who takes the easy ones in your name and pockets what is offered.

events.text: A star has come loose from the heavens and is falling, slowly, the way stars do up here. Its path ends at the shrine town below that has prayed to you for longer than it has had a name. It will land in nine days.
events.arc: A Star Falls Toward the Shrine Town

choices.text: Catch it

ok.log: It is heavy, and hot, and does not want to be caught. You catch it anyway, a day above the town, and set it in your garden. It glows there at night. The town thinks it saw a comet.

fail.log: It burns through your hands and slows, and slows, and lands in a lake outside the town with a hiss heard for miles. Nobody is hurt but you. Your palms remember it for a century.

choices.text: Nudge it toward the empty sea

effects.log: One small push, nine days early, is worth a great shove on the eighth. It falls into the sea in a column of steam, far from anyone.

choices.text: Warn the town in a dream to go to the hills

effects.log: Everyone goes up the hills with picnic baskets to watch. The star lands in an empty field. The town has a new lake and a festival.

events.text: Long ago the people below built you a tomb, though you never died: a great mound with a stone road and stone animals. It is empty. This century, grave robbers have dug into it at last, and found nothing but a teapot. They are standing in the dark, very confused.

choices.text: Let the teapot be their treasure

effects.log: They sell it in the market for a fortune, as the teapot of the immortal. It is a perfectly ordinary teapot. It makes very good tea for its new owner, whom you rather like.

choices.text: Speak in the dark, very quietly

effects.log: "Put it back." They put it back. They also fill in the tunnel, plant flowers on it and become, in time, the tomb's most devoted keepers.

choices.text: Wonder who left a teapot in your tomb

effects.log: You search your memory for a long time. An old friend, at the building, who knew you would not be inside and wanted you to have tea anyway. You had forgotten. You are glad you remembered.

events.text: A prayer rises with an old phrase in it, one you have not heard in a thousand years: the words you swore to a carter named Ma, who pulled you out of a river. You promised to guard his line for as long as you lived. You are still alive. His forty-third great-granddaughter is in trouble.
events.arc: The Oath to the Ma Family

choices.text: Keep the oath: send help at once

effects.log: A flood is coming down on her village. You turn it, very gently, into the next valley, which is empty. She never knows. The oath holds.

choices.text: Look first at what she needs

effects.log: Not rescue. A loan, a bad landlord, a mill she is about to lose. Small trouble. You watch her fight it, and make a note to watch again.

events.text: The Ma line again, a lifetime later. This time the descendant is a boy who wants to be a swordsman and has no teacher, no money and no talent anyone can see. He trains alone at night by the river where his ancestor pulled you out.
events.arc: The Oath to the Ma Family

choices.text: Teach him in his dreams, one form a year

effects.log: Ten years, ten forms. He wins a small tournament at thirty and cannot explain where he learned it. He says a river taught him. Close enough.

choices.text: Send a real teacher his way

effects.log: A wandering master stops at the river for no reason she can name. She sees the boy. She stays. The oath, you think, is mostly about knowing whom to send.

events.text: The last of the Ma line, an old woman with no children, burns incense at the river and says your name, the old one. She knows the story. She says the line ends with her, and she thanks you for a thousand years of keeping it, and asks you to rest now.
events.arc: The Oath to the Ma Family

choices.text: Accept her release with a bow

effects.log: You bow to the river from above the clouds. The oath lifts off you like a wet cloak. You had forgotten it weighed anything at all.

choices.text: Promise to keep watching the river anyway

effects.log: No line to guard, only a river and a carter's memory. You keep watching. It costs nothing, and the river is very beautiful in autumn.

events.text: As a child below you planted a pine seed in a cracked pot at a temple gate. It is still there, the last living thing that knew you when you were small. This year, through the clouds, you see its needles going brown. It is very, very old.

choices.text: Pour your qi down to it like rain

effects.log: It greens a little. A little is a lot, for a tree that old. The monks at the gate cannot understand why it has rallied. They bow to it now.

choices.text: Let it age as you once did

effects.log: It has had longer than almost anything. You watch it the way you would sit at a friend's bedside, without trying to fix it.

events.text: The old pine has fallen in a winter storm. But at its foot, in the same cracked pot, a seedling has come up from one of its cones: a small green thing with three needles. A novice monk is watering it with a teacup.

choices.text: Bless the seedling, quietly

effects.log: Nothing visible. It simply never gets sick, in all the centuries after. The novice grows old caring for it and says it has a good heart.

choices.text: Watch the novice instead of the tree

effects.log: A small person watering a small tree with great care. You did exactly that, once. Some things go on by being handed down a teacup at a time.

events.text: Two great sects of the righteous path are at war below. Both were founded by students of students of your students. Both carry your name on their banners. Each has burned a prayer asking you to curse the other.

choices.text: Curse neither; bless both the same

effects.log: Both get rain on their fields and a quiet month. Both are furious with you. It is a start: they agree on something.

choices.text: Look for where they split

effects.log: A single commentary, nine hundred years ago, on one line you wrote about the sword. One sect read it as patience, the other as speed. You meant both.

events.text: The war has gone on eleven years. A battle is coming at a ford. You can see both commanders praying in their tents. Each holds a copy of the same old line of yours, worn soft with reading.

choices.text: Send both commanders the same dream: the full line

effects.log: Patience and speed, together, the way you wrote it. They meet at the ford at dawn without armies, each holding the same page. They talk until noon.

choices.text: Swell the river so nobody can cross

effects.log: The ford floods for a month. Nobody fights in a flood. In the waiting the soldiers start trading rice across the water.

events.text: Peace below. The two sects have sworn it at the ford, on your name. The heads have asked one more thing: that you write down, once and for all, what you meant by that line about the sword.

choices.text: Write it plainly, in your own hand

effects.log: You write: Be slow until it is time to be fast. A crane takes it down. The sects build a shrine for it. Within a century there are four commentaries on what it means.

choices.text: Write nothing: let them keep arguing in peace

effects.log: An argument with no war in it is just a school. They argue for another thousand years, at dinner, happily.

events.text: Smoke from the founder's hall reaches your isle with a voice in it. The new head of the sect you founded is kneeling at your memorial tablet, introducing themselves to you, as every head does on the first day. This one is the nineteenth. You have watched all nineteen kneel.

choices.text: Answer with a sign: the tablet glows once

effects.log: The candle flames stand straight up and turn gold. The new head nearly faints. The elders talk about it for a generation. It was a small thing. It was the right thing.

choices.text: Listen to what the new head promises

effects.log: Fewer rules, more rice, a new roof on the library. Good promises. You make a note to see which ones are kept.

choices.text: Remember the first head, your own pupil

effects.log: Your first heir knelt in a hall with a leaking roof and no tablet. Nineteen heads later, the roof is gold. The leak, you suspect, is still there.

events.text: The sect you founded has a bad head this century. Not wicked: idle. The training yard grows weeds, the treasury pays for banquets, the good disciples leave. At the founder's festival the head reads your rules aloud and does not hear a word of them.

choices.text: Send the head a long dream of the founding

effects.log: Cold nights, one pot of rice for eleven people, a roof that leaked. The head wakes ashamed and pulls weeds for a month. It does not last. A month is something.

choices.text: Send a sign to the best young disciple instead

effects.log: A feather on the training-yard post, every morning, where only one disciple trains at dawn. Twenty years later that disciple is head. Patience is a founder's art.

choices.text: Let the sect find its own way back

effects.log: Sects are like rivers. They silt up and then they flood and clear. The next head is very good. You did nothing at all, and you are proud of them.

events.text: You watch the sect's morning drills through the clouds and finally understand why the third stance looks wrong. A copyist, five hundred years ago, dropped one stroke from your manual. Bend the knee became break the knee. They have been doing it very bravely ever since.
events.arc: A Typo, Five Hundred Years Old

choices.text: Send the correct stroke in a dream

effects.log: The head wakes, checks the oldest copy, and goes pale. The stance is fixed. The sect's bonesetter retires early. Nobody can find the copyist's grave to complain.

choices.text: Watch: perhaps they improved it

effects.log: The broken stance has evolved into something odd and strong. Five hundred years of brave knees. You do not correct it. You learn it.

choices.text: Laugh, then fix it gently

effects.log: A gust of wind through the library opens the oldest manual at the right page, every morning, for a month. Eventually someone looks.

events.text: Your old room at the sect is kept exactly as you left it: the cracked cup, the bad mattress, the window that sticks. Once a year the disciples compete for the honour of sweeping it. This year two of them are fighting over the broom.

choices.text: Make the broom split in two

effects.log: It snaps cleanly down the middle. They each sweep half the room. Everyone agrees it was a sign. It was.

choices.text: Let the better sweeper win

effects.log: The quiet one wins, because the loud one is busy arguing. That is the whole lesson. You hope someone notices.

choices.text: Look at the cracked cup a long time

effects.log: You drank from it every morning for two hundred years. They keep it on a silk cushion now. It was never a good cup. It was yours.

events.text: The head of the sect you founded has a hard choice: a richer sect offers to merge, bringing money, land and an end to hunger, but the founder's name would come second on the gate. The head burns incense for three nights, asking you.

choices.text: Answer: take the merger; feed them

effects.log: Your name goes second on the gate. The disciples eat three meals a day for the first time in a generation. You find you do not miss the first place on a gate.

choices.text: Answer: keep the name and stay free

effects.log: Lean years. Proud years. In the end they come through on their own. The richer sect collapses a century later. Some choices only look right afterwards.

choices.text: Give no answer: the choice is theirs

effects.log: The head waits three more nights, then stands up and decides. That was what the nights were for. You were only the excuse.

events.text: Fire on the mountain below. A warlord's army is at the gate of the sect you founded, and the gate will not hold till morning. Inside, the head has gathered the children in the founder's hall, in front of your tablet.

choices.text: Send a storm down on the army

ok.log: Lightning walks along the warlord's line and touches no one. Every banner burns. Every horse bolts. By dawn the army is a rumour.

fail.log: Reaching that far down tears at something in you. The storm comes, smaller than you meant. It is enough. You feel it for a decade.

choices.text: Wake the oldest disciple with the secret path

effects.log: There is a cave path behind the hall you dug with your own hands, centuries ago. Everyone has forgotten it. You remind one person. Everyone gets out.

choices.text: Trust the walls you built

effects.log: You built them thick. You built them for exactly this night. They hold until dawn, and at dawn the army goes looking for an easier mountain.

events.text: The sect commissions a new portrait of its founder every two hundred years, each copied from the last. You see the newest one. Somewhere along the way you have become seven feet tall, with a beard to the waist and the eyes of a hungry tiger.

choices.text: Send the painter a dream of your real face

effects.log: The painter wakes and paints a plain, tired, kind face. The elders reject it at once. Too ordinary. It hangs in the kitchen. The cooks like it.

choices.text: Leave the tiger eyes; they work

effects.log: Discipline in the sect improves remarkably. Nobody slacks under those eyes. You were never that frightening. Perhaps you should have been.

choices.text: Ask yourself who the portrait is for

effects.log: Not for you. For a sect that needs a founder bigger than any of its troubles. You let them have the beard.

events.text: You listen in on the new outer disciples at their supper. They know the founder's rules, the founder's hall, the founder's festival. They argue over whether the founder was a real person at all. Nobody at the table knows your name.

choices.text: Hold the forgetting gently

effects.log: The rules live. The hall stands. The name was only a handle. You built something that does not need you. That was the whole plan.

choices.text: Drop your name into one dream

effects.log: One disciple wakes saying it aloud. Nobody believes the dream, but the name is in the sect again, passed from bunk to bunk as a ghost story.

choices.text: Laugh: not a real person

effects.log: You check, carefully. You are fairly sure you are a real person. It is good to be asked, after all this time.

events.text: The elders of the sect you founded hold a council on what you meant. It is about one sentence you wrote in a hurry, in winter, with cold hands, about the tea ration. Three schools of thought have grown up around it. The council has lasted nine days.

choices.text: Send the true meaning in a dream

effects.log: It meant: buy more tea. The eldest elder wakes, laughs for an hour, and closes the council. The tea ration doubles.

choices.text: Let them argue; it trains their minds

effects.log: Nine days of fine argument about tea. Several elders reach new understandings of the sword through it. You did not intend that. You will take the credit.

choices.text: Be glad they read it at all

effects.log: Hundreds of years, and they still read every word you left. You never thought anything you wrote would be read twice.

events.text: The holiest relic of the sect you founded is the Founder's Sword, kept in a jade case and shown once a generation. It is not your sword. Your real sword, nicked and plain, is in the sect kitchen, where the cooks have used it for nine hundred years to stir the soup.

choices.text: Let the cooks keep stirring

effects.log: The soup at that sect is famous across three provinces. Nobody knows why. You know why. Some relics should be useful.

choices.text: Send a dream to the head about the kitchen

effects.log: The head finds the sword in the soup and has it moved to the jade case. The soup is never as good again. The cooks are bitter for a century.

choices.text: Wonder whose sword the jade one is

effects.log: You look closely. It belonged to the bandit you beat to win the sect's first mountain. The sect has been venerating your worst enemy's sword for a thousand years. You decide not to mention it.

events.text: The sect you founded has nine branch schools now, spread across the land. Each claims to be the true heir of the founder. Each has a slightly different story of your life. This year all nine heads have burned petitions to you on the same day, each asking you to name the true one.

choices.text: Name all nine true

effects.log: Nine heads wake from the same dream of a single tree with nine branches. They are all unhappy. They meet to complain about it, together, for the first time in four hundred years.

choices.text: Name the smallest branch, out of mischief

effects.log: A school of twelve disciples in a fishing village is suddenly the true heir. The other eight are scandalised. The twelve are mostly confused. They do well.

choices.text: Look for the one that kept the kitchen rule

effects.log: Only one still feeds every beggar at the gate before the disciples eat. You do not say anything. You just look at that branch more often.

events.text: Hard centuries. The sect you founded has shrunk to three disciples in a half-ruined hall. They cannot afford incense. They still ring the bell at dawn, as you did, and eat one meal a day, as you did in the first winter.

choices.text: Send them a good harvest from the old terraces

effects.log: The terraces nobody has planted in a century come up green on their own. The three eat well. A fourth arrives in spring, then a fifth.

choices.text: Visit the eldest in a dream and say: enough

effects.log: Enough is three people and a bell. That is how it started. The eldest wakes and rings the bell with both hands.

choices.text: Watch, and trust the bell

effects.log: You rang it alone for six years before the first disciple came. They will ring it until someone hears. Someone always does.

events.text: Someone has climbed the white jade stairs today wearing the badge of the sect you founded. {npc}, its thirty-first head, broke through at the end of a long life and has come up into the Upper Realm. {He} is looking around for the founder, with a very old drawing of a giant with tiger eyes.
events.arc: A Disciple of Your Line Ascends

choices.text: Introduce yourself

effects.log: {npc} looks at the drawing. Looks at you. Looks at the drawing. "You are much shorter," {he} says, and then bows so low {he} nearly falls off the isle.

choices.text: Ask for news of the sect

effects.log: {npc} talks for three days. Who married whom, which hall burned, which disciple is promising. You have not had gossip from home in centuries. It is better than any elixir.

choices.text: Show {him} round the Upper Realm

effects.log: The founder of a sect, still teaching the newcomers where the good tea is. {npc} writes it all down for no one. Some habits survive ascension.

events.text: The first manual of the sect you founded, the one you wrote by hand, was carried up with you when you ascended. Word has got out among the immortals. Tonight a shadow is on your isle, moving toward the shelf where it lies.
events.arc: A Thief After the Founding Manual

choices.text: Catch the thief in the act

ok.log: You catch a wrist in the dark. A young immortal, very embarrassed, who only wanted to read the book that built a sect. You let them read it, with you watching.

fail.log: The thief is fast and slippery and gets a fist into your ribs before leaping off the isle, empty-handed. The manual stays. Your ribs complain for a decade.

choices.text: Leave a note on the shelf: ask and I will lend it

effects.log: The shadow stops at the shelf, reads the note, and stands there a long time. Next week a polite letter comes asking to borrow it. You lend it.

choices.text: Let the alarm array do its work

effects.log: Bells, light, a net of qi. The thief is caught upside down until morning. It is a very old array. It still works. So do you.

events.text: Trouble at the sect you founded. The sword hall and the qi hall have stopped eating together. The sword hall says the founder taught the blade first. The qi hall says the founder taught breath first. Both are quoting you. Both are half right.

choices.text: Send both hall masters the same dream

effects.log: In the dream you are breathing and cutting at the same time. They wake and argue about the dream instead. It is progress, of a kind.

choices.text: Wait and see how deep it goes

effects.log: Deeper than one dream. Two kitchens now. Two gates. You watch, uneasily, as a founder watches.

events.text: The sword hall has left. They have built a new sect on the next mountain, with your name on its gate, and call the old one a sect of sleepers. The old one calls them a sect of butchers. There is a skirmish at the stream between the two mountains. Nobody dies. Yet.

choices.text: Send rain to stop the skirmish

effects.log: A cold rain falls only on the stream. Both sides go home soaked and furious, and alive. That is what you wanted from it.

choices.text: Visit the young hothead who struck first

effects.log: In the dream you show the hothead the founding winter: eleven people, one pot of rice, sword people and breath people sharing it. The hothead wakes crying and does not know why.

events.text: A generation on. The two sects trade insults, not blows. But a plague has come to the valley below both mountains, and the qi hall knows medicine while the sword hall knows the roads. Neither will ask the other first.

choices.text: Make them meet at the founding stone

effects.log: Both heads dream of the same stone at the same hour. Both go there to prove the other wrong. They find each other. They find the plague maps. They work all night.

choices.text: Send a sign to the villagers instead

effects.log: The villagers walk up both mountains at once and sit at both gates. Shamed together, the two sects come down together.

events.text: After the plague the two sects did not reunite. But they have built a bridge over the stream between their mountains, and on the founder's day they cross it, both ways, and practise the opening form together: sword and breath, as you taught it, as one.

choices.text: Watch the whole form from the clouds

effects.log: Two hundred people, two schools, one form. Some of the sword people breathe better than the breath people. Some of the breath people cut better. You never needed one sect. You needed this.

choices.text: Send a feather to land on the bridge

effects.log: One white feather, in the middle of the bridge, at the moment the form ends. Both heads bend for it at once. They keep it in a box that belongs to neither.

events.text: The founding stone of the sect, the rock where you first sat to teach, has cracked through in a frost. The elders want to replace it with a polished slab of jade with your name in gold. The younger disciples want to keep the broken rock.

choices.text: Side with the young: a rock is a rock

effects.log: A dream for the eldest elder: you, sitting on a cold rock, teaching eleven hungry people. The jade slab is cancelled. The rock is mended with iron staples.

choices.text: Let them choose; watch who chooses well

effects.log: A long argument, a vote, a compromise: the jade slab beside the broken rock. Nobody sits on the jade.

events.text: Mending the founding stone, a young disciple has found something under it: a scratch in the rock, half worn away, in a hand nobody knows. It is your name, the first time you wrote it in the sect, with a small, bad drawing of a teapot beside it.

choices.text: Let the teapot be famous

effects.log: The teapot becomes the sect's second emblem. It is stitched on the sleeves. Rival sects mock it. Your disciples wear it with pride.

choices.text: Send the disciple a dream of the day you drew it

effects.log: A hot day, an empty mountain, one teapot and nobody to share it. You drew it to have company. The disciple wakes and makes tea for everyone.

events.text: The sect has decided to begin each new disciple's first day at the founding stone, sitting on the cold rock, drinking a cup of tea from a cracked pot. It is the newest tradition, and in a hundred years everyone will say the founder started it.

choices.text: Accept the credit, for once

effects.log: The founder started it, after a fashion, with a bad drawing. You allow yourself to be pleased.

choices.text: Watch the first new disciple drink

effects.log: A small, frightened child with a big cup, sitting where you sat. The tea is terrible. The child drinks all of it. The sect will be fine.

events.text: Pilgrims climb to your hermitage every spring, three days on foot, to see a living master of a thousand years. Most of them only want to look at you. One brought a sick goat. One brought a poem about you, four hundred lines long, in a terrible hand.
events.arc: The Hermit They Climb To See

choices.text: Heal the goat

effects.log: A cough, nothing more. The goat's owner tells the whole province you raise the dead. Next spring there are eleven goats.

choices.text: Hear the whole poem

effects.log: Four hundred lines. Line two hundred and twelve is actually very good. You tell the poet which one. The poet weeps.

choices.text: Sit where they can see you, and say nothing

effects.log: They look. You look back. Something goes between you that is better than advice. They go down the mountain lighter.

events.text: The heads of two righteous sects have climbed to your hermitage together, which they have not done in living memory, because they cannot agree on anything else. They want the oldest master in the murim to judge their quarrel over a ferry.

choices.text: Judge the ferry fairly

effects.log: Mornings to one, evenings to the other, the ferryman's wage from both. They grumble all the way down. The ruling holds for three hundred years.

choices.text: Make them run the ferry together for a month

effects.log: Two sect heads poling a ferry together. By the second week they have opinions about the current. By the fourth they are friends, a little.

choices.text: Send them home to judge it themselves

effects.log: "You are both heads. Be heads." They are offended for an afternoon. On the road down, they settle it.

events.text: News climbs your mountain: a merchant has died at a hundred and ten, the last person below who knew you before you were a legend. As a boy he sold you dumplings. He told his grandchildren you overpaid. You did.

choices.text: Go to the funeral as a stranger

effects.log: Nobody knows the old visitor at the back. You light incense. His great-grandchildren serve dumplings to the mourners. You overpay again, by leaving coins under the plate.

choices.text: Sit alone with it a while

effects.log: Nobody alive has seen you young now. It feels like a door closing in another part of the house. You sit until it stops echoing.

choices.text: Buy dumplings at the stall his family still runs

effects.log: Same stall, same street. The dumplings are better than his were. You do not tell them that. You tell them they are just as good.

events.text: A famous young hero has climbed your mountain to prove that the legend is only a legend. {npc} has won every duel in the land and would like one more on the list: the master who has been alive for a thousand years.
events.arc: The Young Hero at the Gate

choices.text: Accept one bout

ok.log: Four moves. {npc} sits on the ground looking at the sky for a long time. Then {he} asks, very quietly, whether you take students.

fail.log: {npc} is truly gifted. {He} lands a blow. You end the bout anyway, sore and delighted. A thousand years, and somebody can still surprise you.

choices.text: Invite {him} to sweep the yard first

effects.log: {npc} sweeps, furious. Then less furious. By evening {he} has noticed how you sweep. The duel is forgotten. The lesson is not.

choices.text: Decline: you have nothing to prove

effects.log: {npc} calls you a coward down the whole mountain. Twenty years later {he} climbs back up, older, to apologise and ask what you meant.

events.text: When you came down from your mountain this year, the valley had a paper mill, a stone bridge, a school and a great many people who have never heard of the old wars. The children call you Grandparent Hermit. Some of their great-great-grandparents called you that too.

choices.text: Teach at the school for a season

effects.log: Reading, counting and how to fall without breaking anything. The last one is the most popular.

choices.text: Walk the new bridge every morning

effects.log: It is a good bridge. You used to wade here with the fish. You find you can love a bridge.

choices.text: Learn how the paper mill works

effects.log: Pulp, screens, sunlight. The papermaker is happy to show the old hermit. You make one sheet. It is lumpy. You keep it.

events.text: You have appointed eleven heads of the sect you founded, one after another, and outlived ten of them. The eleventh is old now and asks to step down. The sect waits for you to choose the twelfth, as it always has.

choices.text: Choose the most able elder

effects.log: A safe choice, a good one. The sect breathes out. You attend the installation, as you have ten times before, and it does not get easier.

choices.text: Choose the youngest, boldest disciple

effects.log: Uproar for a year. Then the sect starts to move again, faster than in a century. You remember being that young and that bold.

choices.text: Let the sect choose without you

effects.log: For the first time the sect votes. They choose well. You realise you could have trusted them a long time ago.

events.text: In a plain robe at dawn, sweeping the outer courtyard because you like to, you are scolded by a new disciple for being slow. The new disciple does not know the founder's face. Hardly anyone does now. The founder's portrait is seven feet tall.

choices.text: Sweep faster, and say nothing

effects.log: Weeks later the disciple sees you on the founder's seat at the festival and drops a tray of cups. You wink. The disciple grows up very polite to sweepers.

choices.text: Hand over the broom and teach a lesson

effects.log: "Show me faster." The disciple tries. You show how to sweep with the breath. The courtyard has never been so clean.

choices.text: Enjoy being nobody

effects.log: Nobody asks the sweeper for judgements or blessings or loans. You sweep the courtyard every morning for a year, happily.

events.text: A young elder lectures the inner disciples on the founder's teaching. You listen from the back of the hall. The lecture is fluent, learned and confident. It explains exactly the opposite of what you meant.

choices.text: Stand up and correct it

effects.log: The hall goes silent. The young elder goes white, then red, then very thoughtful. A good teacher, it turns out, who can learn.

choices.text: Ask a question that lets the elder find it

effects.log: One question. The elder stops mid-sentence, frowns, and turns the lecture around. The disciples think the elder is brilliant. The elder knows better and comes to thank you.

choices.text: Wonder whether the elder's meaning is better

effects.log: It might be. You wrote that line at forty, in a hurry. The elder read it at two hundred, slowly. You go away to think.

events.text: The sect has made relics of your old things while you are still using them. Your walking stick is in a glass case. Your teacup is on an altar. You would very much like your teacup back.

choices.text: Take the teacup back

effects.log: The keeper of relics follows you all morning in anguish. At noon you return it and buy a new one. The new one becomes a relic within the year.

choices.text: Use the relics as relics: teach with them

effects.log: You give a lecture on the stick, how it is worn on one side from the bad knee. The disciples learn more from the stick than from the scrolls.

choices.text: Laugh, and let them have it all

effects.log: A sect needs things to hold. You have a body to hold. You drink from a plain bowl and feel lighter than you have in centuries.

events.text: The elders of the sect you founded come to you together with a very carefully worded request. You are revered. You are beloved. You are, perhaps, too old to sit on every council. Would the founder consider a quieter pavilion, higher up the mountain?
events.arc: The Elders Want You to Rest

choices.text: Agree, and move up the mountain

effects.log: The pavilion has a view and no councils. Within a year the elders are climbing up to ask your advice anyway. Now they have to climb.

choices.text: Refuse, politely and permanently

effects.log: "I built the council chamber. I will sit in it." They bow. You sit in it. You are very good at councils. That is the problem.

choices.text: Ask which elder wrote the request

effects.log: The youngest. Brave, careful, right about most of it. You make that elder head of the council. The others did not expect that.
